question.prompt: Consider the graphs of \((1)\) \(y=x^2-\dfrac12x+2\) and \((2)\) \(y=x^2+\dfrac12x+2\) on the same set of axes. These parabolas have exactly the same shape. Then:

solutions.explanation:
Completing the square reveals each parabola's position while preserving its shape:
\[
\begin{aligned}
(1)\quad y&=\left(x-\frac14\right)^2+\frac{31}{16},\\
(2)\quad y&=\left(x+\frac14\right)^2+\frac{31}{16}.
\end{aligned}
\]
In the form \(y=(x-h)^2+k\), the vertex is \((h,k)\). Thus the two vertices are
\[
\left(\frac14,\frac{31}{16}\right)
\quad\text{and}\quad
\left(-\frac14,\frac{31}{16}\right).
\]
The squared terms have the same coefficient and the vertices have the same height. Graph (1) is therefore graph (2) shifted horizontally by
\[
\frac14-\left(-\frac14\right)=\frac12
\]
unit to the right. The answer is \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).
